subsection: 2. Dietary requirements through the life cycle

notes.b: No two people need exactly the same diet. Energy and nutrient needs change with the stage of life and with circumstances, so every meal plan starts from the requirements of the person it is for.
points: A balanced diet contains all the nutrients in the correct proportions for the individual's needs and good health, so what counts as balanced differs from person to person.
Age: needs change at each life stage, with growth in childhood and adolescence, maintenance in adults and falling energy needs in older age.
Sex: men generally need more energy than women because they have greater muscle mass and a larger body, while girls and women need extra iron once menstruation begins.
Health status: illness, allergy, diabetes or a digestive disorder can change the foods a person is allowed to eat or how well their body absorbs nutrients.
Pregnancy and breastfeeding increase the need for energy, protein, folate, iron and calcium, because the body is building a baby or making milk.
Activity: energy needs rise with physical activity, and active people also need more fluid and carbohydrate. A sedentary adult needs less energy.
Energy balance: energy taken in as food should match energy used by the body; any surplus is stored as body fat.
notes.tip: Exams ask for the factors affecting an adolescent's requirements: age, activity level, gender, health status, pregnancy and faddy eating (choosing only a few favourite foods). Name each factor and say what it changes.

notes.b: A baby's first food and a young child's meals are planned around fast growth, a small stomach and teeth that are still forming. Pre-school guidelines are examined as short lists of practical rules.
points: Breast milk supplies all the nutrients a baby needs for about the first six months.
Breastfed babies, and babies taking little formula, are advised to take a vitamin D supplement from birth to 12 months, because breast milk contains little vitamin D.
Weaning (moving from milk to solid food) begins at about six months, when the iron stored at birth starts to run low. Puréed meat and iron-fortified cereals supply iron.
Salt should be kept low and sugar limited in foods for babies and young children, with none added to baby foods. Sugar harms developing teeth.

Pre-school children have small, variable appetites, so regular balanced meals in small, manageable portions with nutritious snacks between suit them better than large meals. Attractive presentation helps.
Young children need protein for growth, calcium and vitamin D for bones and teeth, iron for blood, and fruit and vegetables, following the Food Pyramid.
Fussy eating is common. Offering new flavours one at a time in small portions, without forcing a child to eat, and involving the child in food preparation, helps them accept new foods.
Sugary foods and drinks should be limited to protect developing teeth.
notes.tip: For three guidelines for pre-school children, pick distinct ones, such as small regular meals, limiting sugary food and drink to protect teeth, and offering new foods without forcing. Link each to its reason.

notes.b: School-age children need every nutrient in balance, and adolescents need even more during the growth spurt. Teenage eating habits, though, often work against meeting those needs.
points: Children need every nutrient in balanced proportions, following the Irish Food Pyramid with portions suited to their age and activity. Protein is for growth, carbohydrate and fat for energy, calcium for bones and teeth, iron for blood, plus fibre and water, with nutritious snacks and less sugar and salt.
Ways to include vegetables for children: stir-fries, cut shapes, grated or blended into sauces, smoothies, soups, and vegetables in lunchboxes.
Adolescents go through a growth spurt, roughly between the ages of 12 and 19, which increases the need for every nutrient.

Girls need extra iron once they begin menstruating, because menstrual blood loss depletes iron stores. Fruit and vegetables supply fibre and vitamin C, and vitamin C improves the absorption of iron from plant foods, helping avoid anaemia.
Calcium and vitamin D build bone mass during adolescence, so good intake now builds peak bone mass and reduces the risk of osteoporosis (weak, brittle bones) later.

Active teenagers need high-energy starchy foods such as pasta, potatoes, rice and wholegrain cereals. Protein from meat, fish, eggs, dairy and pulses (animal and plant sources) supports growth and repair.

High-salt, high-sugar and high-fat snacks and fizzy drinks add energy but few nutrients, so they should be limited. Irregular meals and skipped breakfasts are common in adolescence and make it harder to meet nutritional needs, so teenagers should eat three varied meals daily and avoid skipping meals, especially breakfast.

Factors making a healthy diet difficult for teenagers: likes and dislikes, early exposure to fatty, salty and sugary foods, convenience and eating on the go, availability, cost, advertising and peers.
notes.tip: Exams ask for four guidelines for teenagers and for changes in teenage eating patterns. Use limiting snacks and fizzy drinks, not skipping breakfast, three varied meals, and iron with vitamin C, each with its reason.

notes.b: Adult bodies are no longer growing, so the aim shifts to maintaining health and weight. The main guideline is to match what you eat to how active you are.
points: Adults need to balance energy intake with activity to maintain a healthy weight, and to eat a balanced diet with all the nutrients in proportion.
Daily starchy foods, fruit and vegetables supply the fibre, vitamins and minerals that support bowel health.
Protein maintains muscle and repairs tissue, so a protein food is included at each main meal.
Unsaturated oils should replace saturated fats, and sugar and salt should be kept low.
Women of childbearing age need adequate folate and iron, because menstrual losses continue.
A sedentary worker (one who sits most of the day) needs less energy, so should reduce fat and sugar, eat fibre-rich foods, get enough calcium, iron and vitamins, and limit salt.
notes.tip: For a sedentary adult, say that energy needs are lower, then give guidelines such as less fat and sugar, more fibre, and limited salt.

notes.b: Older bodies burn less energy but still need nearly as many nutrients, so food must be nutrient-dense. Practical problems with teeth, appetite and money also shape what older people can eat.
points: Energy needs fall with age because muscle mass and activity decline, so portions should be smaller but nutrient-dense (packed with nutrients per mouthful). Small, frequent, appetising meals suit reduced appetite, and fortified foods help.
Protein remains important for maintaining muscle and repairing tissue, so older people should include a protein food at main meals.
Calcium and vitamin D protect the bones, and calcium absorption decreases with age.
Vitamin B12 absorption can fall in later life, so older people may need B12 from fortified foods or supplements.
Fibre and fluid prevent constipation, which is common among older people who are less active. Iron and vitamin C are also needed.
Salt should be reduced to help control blood pressure, and saturated fat reduced.
Chewing and swallowing difficulties, or dentures, call for soft, moist and easy-to-chew foods. A limited budget and reduced mobility also affect shopping and cooking.
Diet-related conditions common in older people include osteoporosis, diabetes, coronary heart disease, high blood pressure and high cholesterol.
notes.tip: When asked to name a diet-related condition affecting older people and a cause, give one condition and a dietary cause, such as osteoporosis from low calcium intake and falling calcium absorption.

notes.b: A pregnant woman's diet must feed her own body and build a baby, so the need for particular nutrients rises while food safety matters more. This is the group examined most often, usually as nutrient, reason and food source.
points: Folic acid (also called folate) taken before conception and in early pregnancy helps prevent neural-tube defects in the developing baby. Sources include green vegetables and fortified cereals, plus a supplement as advised.
Iron supports the extra blood volume of pregnancy and the baby's iron stores; vitamin C eaten at the same meal improves iron absorption.
Calcium and vitamin D are needed for the baby's bones and teeth and to protect the mother's bones.
Protein from lean meat, fish, fully cooked eggs and pasteurised dairy supports the growth of fetal tissue, the placenta and maternal tissues.
Omega-3 fatty acids from cooked oily fish, such as salmon, support the development of the baby's brain and nervous system. Iodine and vitamins A, C, D, K and folate are also needed.

Water is needed for blood plasma and fetal tissues, to carry nutrients and remove waste, and to prevent dehydration and constipation. Fibre also helps prevent constipation, which is common in pregnancy.

Energy needs rise only modestly, mainly in later pregnancy, so a pregnant woman should not double her food intake. She should balance food with activity, follow the Food Pyramid and choose low-GI starchy foods.
Breastfeeding women need extra energy, protein, calcium and fluid to produce milk.
notes.tip: For a question on four dietary requirements of pregnant women, give the nutrient, the reason and a food source for each, such as folic acid, iron with vitamin C, calcium with vitamin D, and omega-3.

notes.h: Foods to avoid in pregnancy and a sample menu
notes.b: Some foods carry bacteria that can harm an unborn baby, so pregnancy guidelines restrict them. Any menu for a pregnant woman must follow these rules.
points: Pâté, unpasteurised milk, soft mould-ripened cheese, and raw or undercooked meat, fish and eggs carry a risk of listeria or salmonella (food-poisoning bacteria) and should be avoided.
Alcohol should be avoided in pregnancy, and caffeine and salt should be limited.
Taste changes and morning sickness can be managed with dry toast before rising and small, frequent meals.
A sample one-day menu uses pasteurised dairy and fully cooked foods. Breakfast: fruit juice, porridge made with pasteurised milk and berries, wholemeal toast.
Lunch: vegetable soup, wholemeal bread, yoghurt and fruit. Dinner: well-cooked lean chicken or fish with vegetables and potatoes.
notes.tip: Never put a risky food in a pregnancy menu: use pasteurised milk and fully cooked meat, fish and eggs, and say why each meal meets a requirement.

notes.b: A convalescent is someone recovering from illness. Their appetite is low but their body needs nutrients to repair itself, so food must be light, appealing and nourishing.
points: Convalescents need small, appetising, easy-to-digest portions, because appetite is often reduced during recovery. Regular balanced meals are important.
Protein from lean meat, fish, eggs and dairy supports tissue repair.
Iron and vitamin C support recovery of blood levels, and vitamin C from fruit and vegetables aids iron absorption. Fibre-rich fruit and vegetables and fluids keep the bowel working.
Lightly seasoned meals are better tolerated; spicy, fried, oily and greasy foods should be avoided.
notes.tip: Do not confuse convalescents with active people. Convalescents need small, light, protein-rich meals, not extra energy and fluid.

notes.b: Active people burn more energy and lose fluid in sweat, so their diet is built around extra fuel and water.
points: Active people need extra energy, mainly from complex carbohydrates such as wholegrain bread, pasta, rice and potatoes.
Sweat losses mean active people need extra fluid, drunk before, during and after exercise.
Protein supports muscle repair and growth after exercise, and fruit, yoghurt or wholegrain sandwiches supply energy between meals.
notes.tip: Active people need extra energy and fluid, not the small light meals of a convalescent. Name complex carbohydrates as the main energy source.

notes.b: Shift work and long or varied days disrupt normal mealtimes. Good planning keeps meals balanced even when no one is home at the usual time.
points: Irregular shifts disrupt mealtimes, so people often skip meals or rely on fast food and vending machines, which should be avoided.
Planning ahead with a list, and keeping staples and some frozen or prepared ingredients, makes balanced meals easier.
Batch cooking and freezing portions allows balanced meals to be eaten at staggered times without much last-minute preparation.
Soups, casseroles and other reheatable portions suit people eating at different times.
Packed lunches with fruit, wholegrain bread and yoghurt keep nutrition on track during long working days.
Slow cookers and timers allow a meal to cook while the household is out. Portions should stay balanced, following the guidelines.
notes.tip: For strategies for families with irregular routines, give a range: planning ahead, batch cooking and freezing, reheatable dishes, slow cooker or timer, and packed meals, each with how it helps.

keyTerms.definition: The relationship between the energy taken in through food and the energy used by the body; a surplus is stored as body fat.
The gradual introduction of solid foods alongside breast milk or formula, usually from about six months.
A period of rapid physical growth in adolescence, roughly between 12 and 19 years, that increases nutrient needs.
The synthetic form of folate, a B vitamin taken before conception and in early pregnancy to protect against neural-tube defects.
A birth defect of the brain or spinal cord, such as spina bifida, which folic acid helps to prevent.
The period of recovery after illness or surgery, when the need for protein and nutrients for repair is high but appetite may be low.
A food-borne infection caused by Listeria bacteria that can seriously harm an unborn baby; risk foods include unpasteurised dairy products and pâté.
A B vitamin found mainly in animal foods that is needed for red blood cells and nerve function.

questions.prompt: Outline three differences between the dietary requirements of a baby and those of a pre-school child.
questions.model: Babies rely on breast milk or formula for most of their nutrition until about six months, whereas pre-school children eat a range of solid foods from the Irish Food Pyramid. Breastfed babies need a vitamin D supplement, while a pre-school child gets vitamin D from food and sunlight. A baby's iron comes from breast milk and iron-fortified weaning foods, while a pre-school child needs iron from meat, fish, pulses and fortified cereals. Babies feed little and often on demand, while pre-school children need regular meals and snacks with a varied diet. Any three differences, each explained, earn 6 marks.

questions.prompt: Discuss the dietary requirements of a pregnant woman and explain how a family could plan meals across a day to meet them.
questions.model: Requirements: protein for fetal and maternal tissues; folic acid before conception and in early pregnancy to prevent neural-tube defects; iron for extra blood volume and fetal stores, with vitamin C at the same meal to aid absorption; calcium and vitamin D for the baby's bones and teeth; omega-3 fatty acids from cooked oily fish for the brain; fibre and fluid to prevent constipation; modest extra energy, mainly later in pregnancy. Food safety: avoid pâté, unpasteurised dairy, soft mould-ripened cheese, raw or undercooked meat and eggs; avoid alcohol; limit caffeine and salt. Meal plan: breakfast of fortified porridge with pasteurised milk and fruit; lunch of lentil and vegetable soup with wholemeal bread and a yoghurt; dinner of thoroughly cooked salmon with potatoes, broccoli and carrots, followed by fresh fruit; water through the day. Each meal combines protein, starch, fruit or vegetables and dairy, and avoids high-risk foods.
